title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, at Sea, during the Month of July, 1819
description: Daily temperature, sea-water temperature and specific gravity, barometer, winds and weather kept aboard Hecla while crossing Baffin's Bay outbound. The first of a run of monthly registers that make up one of the earliest sustained instrumental weather series for the Canadian Arctic archipelago.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, at Sea, during the Month of August, 1819
description: Monthly weather abstract kept as Hecla worked through Lancaster Sound and Barrow Strait toward Melville Island.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of September, 1819
description: Weather abstract covering the crossing of 110 degrees west and the ships' entry into Winter Harbour, where they were beset for the winter on 26 September 1819.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of November, 1819
description: Monthly weather abstract from the first full month frozen in at Winter Harbour, Melville Island, as the polar night closed in.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of December, 1819
description: Weather abstract kept through the depth of the Arctic winter at Winter Harbour, including the coldest temperatures the expedition recorded.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of February, 1820
description: Monthly weather abstract from Winter Harbour as the sun began to reappear over Melville Island.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of April, 1820
description: Weather abstract from Winter Harbour as the crews prepared for the sledging excursions across Melville Island.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of May, 1820
description: Monthly weather abstract from Winter Harbour in the month the overland excursions to the north coast of Melville Island were made.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, during the Month of July, 1820
description: Weather abstract from the final weeks at Winter Harbour before the ice released the ships in early August 1820.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, at Sea, during the Month of August, 1820
description: Weather abstract from the ships' escape from Winter Harbour and passage back east through the pack ice of Barrow Strait.

title: Abstract of the Meteorological Journal kept on board His Majesty's Ship Hecla, at Sea, during the Month of September, 1820
description: Weather abstract from the homeward passage through Davis Strait and Baffin's Bay toward England.

title: Appendix No. I: An Account of the Going of the Chronometers of the Hecla and Griper
description: Title page introducing the chronometer appendix, which used eight chronometers to fix longitude throughout the voyage and, cross-checked against lunar distances, established the position of Winter Harbour and the discoveries along Melville Island's coast.

title: Going of the Chronometers: comparison of rates at the Calton Hill Observatory and the resulting longitude of Melville Island
description: Narrative explaining how comparison of the four best chronometers against the Calton Hill Observatory, Edinburgh, fixed the error of Greenwich time and so the longitude of the western parts of Melville Island and part of Baffin's Bay and Davis Strait surveyed in 1820.

title: Table I: An Account of the going of the undermentioned Chronometers, on Mean Greenwich Time, during a Trial of Five Weeks previous to their embarkation
description: Pre-voyage trial of the ships' Arnold and Parkinson & Frodsham chronometers at London in April-May 1819, the baseline against which every later rate at sea and at Winter Harbour was measured.

title: Table No. II: the going of the chronometers from the commencement of the Voyage to the close of the season of Navigation of 1819, average Daily Rate
description: Summary of chronometer performance across the whole outbound passage of 1819, from departure to the ships' beset at Winter Harbour.

title: Table III: An Account of the going of the under-mentioned Chronometers on Mean Greenwich Time, from the commencement of the Voyage to the close of the Navigation in 1819
description: Week-by-week chronometer rates, May to September 1819, for Arnold's and Parkinson & Frodsham's instruments, with air and sea temperatures noted alongside each comparison.

title: Table III: An Account of the going of the under-mentioned Chronometers on Mean Greenwich Time, from the commencement of the Voyage to the close of the Navigation in 1819 (continued)
description: Continuation of the weekly chronometer-rate table for the 1819 outbound passage.

title: Table IV: An Account of the going of the Hecla's Chronometers on Mean Time at Winter Harbour, from September 30th, 1819, to April 27th, 1820
description: Nearly seven months of chronometer rates recorded through the polar winter at Winter Harbour, the data used to fix the longitude of Melville Island against Greenwich.

title: Table V: the going of the chronometers on Mean Time at Winter Harbour during the Twelve Weeks preceding the season of Navigation of 1820
description: Chronometer rates for the final weeks before break-up, used to carry the Winter Harbour longitude forward into the 1820 sailing season.

title: Table VII: A Statement of the Daily Rates of the under-mentioned Chronometers in London, since their return from the Expedition
description: Chronometer performance re-tested in London after the ships came home, checking the instruments' Melville Island rates still held after the voyage's shocks and cold.

title: Appendix No. II: Lunar Observations
description: Title page for the appendix recording 692 sets of lunar-distance observations (6,982 individual distances) taken to fix longitude independent of the chronometers, cross-checking the chronometer-derived position of Winter Harbour.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, at Sea, 1819
description: Raw lunar-distance sights (star or sun to moon) taken from on board Hecla while crossing Davis Strait in June 1819, used to compute longitude by the lunar-distance method.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, at Sea, 1819 (continued)
description: Continuing series of lunar-distance sights taken at sea during the 1819 outbound passage.

title: Lunar Observations at Sea, August 12th to 15th inclusive, 1819
description: Lunar-distance sights taken as Hecla worked west through Barrow Strait toward Melville Island in mid-August 1819.

title: Lunar Observations at Sea, August 18th to the 19th inclusive, 1819
description: Lunar-distance sights from the final approach to Melville Island before the ships reached Winter Harbour.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1819
description: Lunar-distance sights taken as the ships closed on and moored at Winter Harbour in the autumn of 1819.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1819 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from the early weeks at Winter Harbour.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1819 (continued)
description: Further lunar-distance sights taken at Winter Harbour before the onset of the deep winter.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, January to April 1820
description: Lunar-distance sights taken from the Observatory House ashore at Winter Harbour across the depth of the polar winter, 1819-1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from the Winter Harbour observatory in early 1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from Winter Harbour, spring 1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from Winter Harbour, spring 1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from Winter Harbour ahead of the 1820 sailing season.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from Winter Harbour, 1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820 (continued)
description: Continuing lunar-distance series from Winter Harbour in the weeks before break-up, 1820.

title: Lunar Observations for the Longitude, 1820, with summary of results
description: Closing table and note: altogether 692 sets, containing 6,982 distances, of which 384 sets were taken from the shore Observatory House and 308 from on board Hecla; averaging all gave the longitude of the Hecla's station at Winter Harbour as 110 degrees 48 minutes 2 seconds west of Greenwich.

title: Appendix No. III: Observations to determine the Latitude, and the Longitude by Chronometers
description: Title page for the appendix of daily noon-position fixes by meridian altitude and chronometer taken throughout the 1819 outward and 1820 homeward passages.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers
description: Running table of the ship's noon latitude and chronometer-derived longitude during the 1819 outward passage through Lancaster Sound and Barrow Strait.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Continuing daily position-fix table for the 1819 outward passage.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Continuing daily position-fix table for the 1819 outward passage.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Continuing daily position-fix table for the 1819 outward passage.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Continuing daily position-fix table for the 1819 outward passage as the ships worked toward Melville Island.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Continuing daily position-fix table for the 1819 outward passage.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers (continued)
description: Final entries of the 1819 outward-passage position-fix table, ending as the ships approached Melville Island.

title: Longitude by each of the Chronometers
description: Comparison table showing the longitude each individual chronometer separately implied for the same fixed point, the check used to weigh the instruments' relative trustworthiness.

title: Observations made in the Winter of 1819, 1820, to ascertain the Error of the Chronometer No. 259 on Mean Time; whence the Longitude of Winter Harbour was deduced from the Lunar Observations in Appendix II. Latitude 74 degrees 47 minutes 13 seconds N.
description: Winter observations of chronometer No. 259's error against apparent time, the link connecting the lunar-distance longitude of Appendix II to the ship's Winter Harbour anchorage.

title: Observations made on board the Hecla
description: Meridian-altitude sun and star sights used to fix latitude, part of the position-determination record supporting the chronometer and lunar longitudes elsewhere in the appendix.

title: Meridian Altitudes: Observations made on board the Hecla, continued
description: Continuing series of meridian-altitude sights for latitude.

title: Observations to ascertain the Error of No. 259 on Mean Time at the Observatory, previous to the Sailing of the Expedition from Winter Harbour in 1820
description: Final check of chronometer No. 259's error at the shore observatory just before the ships broke free of Winter Harbour in 1820, carrying the winter's longitude work forward into the return voyage.

title: Latitudes, and Longitudes by Chronometers
description: Running position-fix table from the 1820 homeward passage, after the ships broke free of Winter Harbour.

title: Appendix No. IV: Abstract of Observations on the Dip of the Horizon at Sea, with Dr. Wollaston's Dip Sector
description: Appendix recording sea-horizon dip measurements taken with Wollaston's dip sector, a correction needed to reduce the ship's latitude and longitude sights to accuracy at high northern latitudes.

title: Observations on the Dip of the Horizon at Sea (continued)
description: Continuing table of sea-horizon dip readings taken with Wollaston's dip sector during the voyage.

title: Appendix No. V: Magnetic Observations
description: Title page for the appendix of magnetic dip, variation and intensity observations, among the first sustained magnetic survey work carried out in the Canadian Arctic archipelago, in a region close enough to the North Magnetic Pole that compass variation changed by tens of degrees between stations.

title: Observations on the Dip
description: Table of magnetic dip (inclination) readings taken over the course of the voyage, tracking the needle's steepening pull toward vertical as the ships closed on the North Magnetic Pole.

title: Abstract of Observations on the Variation, made on Shore, or on the Ice
description: Compass-variation readings taken standing on land or on the sea ice rather than aboard ship, avoiding the iron of the vessel's own structure.

title: Abstract of Observations on the Variation, made on Shore, or on the Ice, continued
description: Shore and ice variation readings dated 23 July 1819 at latitude 73 degrees 03 minutes N, with variation exceeding 82 degrees west, a measure of how sharply the compass was already being pulled by the nearby Magnetic Pole.

title: Abstract of Observations on the Variation, made on Shore, or on the Ice, continued
description: Continuing series of shore and ice compass-variation readings.

title: Observations to determine the Variation, during an Excursion into the Interior of Melville Island, North Georgia
description: Compass-variation readings taken during the overland sledging excursion across the interior of Melville Island in 1820, part of Parry's push to survey and understand the magnetism of the region around the North Magnetic Pole.

title: Observations to determine the Variation at Winter Harbour, Melville Island, Latitude 74 degrees 47 minutes 13 seconds N., Longitude 110 degrees 49 minutes 0 seconds W.
description: Systematic compass-variation readings taken at the fixed shore station at Winter Harbour, the expedition's base observatory for the winter of 1819-1820.

title: Observations on the Variation made on Shore, or on Ice, during the Navigation of 1820
description: Compass-variation readings taken on land or ice during the 1820 sailing season, as the ships worked home through the archipelago.

title: Observations on the Variation, made at Sea, in H.M.S. Hecla, 1819, continued
description: Shipboard compass-variation readings from the 1819 outward passage.

title: Observations on the Variation, made at Sea, in H.M.S. Hecla, 1819, continued
description: Shipboard variation readings dated 13 June 1819 at latitude 57 degrees 55 minutes N, longitude 40 degrees 57 minutes W, in the North Atlantic on the crossing to Davis Strait.

title: Observations on the Variation, made at Sea, in H.M.S. Hecla, 1819, continued
description: Continuing shipboard compass-variation readings from the 1819 outward passage.

title: Observations on the Variation, made at Sea, in H.M.S. Hecla, 1819, continued
description: Continuing shipboard compass-variation readings from the 1819 outward passage.

title: Observations on the Variation, made at Sea, in H.M.S. Hecla, 1819, continued
description: Continuing shipboard compass-variation readings as the ships worked west through Lancaster Sound in 1819.

title: Observations on the Variation, made in H.M.S. the Hecla, 1820
description: Shipboard variation readings dated 4 September 1820 at latitude 71 degrees 10 minutes N, longitude 70 degrees 42 minutes W, on the homeward passage across Baffin's Bay.

title: Observations on the Intensity of the Magnetic Force, with Mr. Browne's Dipping-Needle, 1819, March. In the Regent's Park, London, Latitude 51 degrees 31 minutes 40 seconds N., Longitude 0 degrees 08 minutes W. Dip 70 degrees 33.3 N.
description: Baseline magnetic-intensity readings taken in London with Browne's dipping needle before departure, the reference against which the Arctic readings were compared.

title: Observations on the Magnetic Force, 1820, December. In the Regent's Park, London, Latitude 51 degrees 31 minutes N., Longitude 0 degrees 08 minutes W. Dip 70 degrees 33.3 N.
description: Magnetic-intensity readings retaken in London after the ships' return, checking whether the dipping needle's London reading had drifted since 1819.

title: Observations on the Magnetic Force, 1819, June 26th. On Ice in Davis' Strait, Latitude 64 degrees N., Longitude 61 degrees 50 minutes W., distant 222 Yards from the Ships; Dip 83 degrees 04 minutes N.
description: Magnetic-intensity reading taken standing on the sea ice of Davis Strait, 222 yards from the ships, showing the dip needle already standing at over 83 degrees so far from home.

title: Observations on the Magnetic Force
description: Magnetic-intensity readings with the dipping needle taken at Winter Harbour in the weeks before the ships sailed in 1820.

title: Appendix No. VI: Table of Days Works kept on board the Hecla
description: Title page for the dead-reckoning log abstract, the ship's day-by-day course, distance and estimated position kept independent of the astronomical fixes elsewhere in the appendix.

title: Abstract of Days Works
description: Dead-reckoning table of the ship's daily course and distance run during the 1819 outward passage.

title: Abstract of Days Works (continued)
description: Continuing dead-reckoning table of the ship's daily course and distance.

title: Abstract of Days Works (continued)
description: Continuing dead-reckoning table, covering the approach to and station at Winter Harbour.

title: Abstract of Days Works (continued)
description: Dead-reckoning table for the 1820 homeward passage after the ships broke free of Winter Harbour.

title: Appendix No. VII: Tide Table in Winter Harbour, Melville Island, 1820
description: Title page for the tide record kept at Winter Harbour, one of the first sustained tidal series taken anywhere in the Canadian Arctic archipelago and still a reference point for tidal studies in the region.

title: Tide Table in Winter Harbour
description: Daily record of high and low water observed at Winter Harbour, Melville Island, through the spring of 1820.

title: Tide Table in Winter Harbour (continued)
description: Continuing daily tide record from Winter Harbour, Melville Island.

title: Tide Table in Winter Harbour, continued
description: Continuing daily tide record from Winter Harbour, Melville Island, running up to the ships' departure.

title: Appendix No. VIII: An Account of Experiments to determine the Acceleration of the Pendulum in Different Latitudes
description: Pendulum-swing experiments carried out at Winter Harbour to measure the local strength of gravity, part of the international program comparing Earth's shape and gravity at different latitudes; high-latitude pendulum data of this kind was still scarce in 1820.

title: Appendix No. IX: Remarks on the State of Health and Disease on Board the Hecla and Griper
description: The expedition surgeons' account of the crews' health through the first deliberate Arctic overwintering by a Royal Navy expedition, including the onset of scurvy late in the winter and the measures, among them fresh sledging exercise and the North Georgia Gazette theatricals, credited with checking it.

title: Chart of Bathurst Island, Lancaster Sound and Barrow's Strait (west sheet)
description: West half of the large folding chart of the newly discovered coasts, showing Bathurst Island, Graham Moore's Bay and the southern shore worked along the outward passage.

title: Chart of Bathurst Island, Lancaster Sound and Barrow's Strait (east sheet)
description: East half of the same folding chart, showing Navy Board Inlet, the Cunninghame Mountains and the western part of Baffin's Bay leading in from Sir James Lancaster's Sound.

title: Views of the coast: Cape Byam Martin Island and the shores of Barrow's Strait
description: Coastal-profile sketches of headlands as they appeared from the deck, drawn to help later navigators recognize the same coast by its silhouette.

title: Views of the coast: Cape Warrender and the North Shore of Sir James Lancaster's Sound and Barrow's Strait
description: Four stacked coastal-profile views by F. W. Beechey, including Cape Warrender bearing N.82 degrees W. and the north shore of Barrow's Strait, engraved for recognition of the coast by future ships.

title: Views of the coast: the Northern Coast of Barrow's Strait, Hobhouse Inlet and Cape Fellfoot
description: Coastal-profile views of the north shore of Barrow's Strait, drawn to help later ships identify the same headlands.

title: Views of the coast: Prince Leopold's Islands, Cape York, and a view in Prince Regent's Inlet
description: Coastal-profile views by F. W. Beechey, including the southernmost and northernmost of Prince Leopold's Islands and Cape York, published by John Murray in 1821.

title: Views of the coast: Cape Hotham, Caswall's Tower, Cape Ricketts, a peak on Bathurst Island, and Cape Cockburn
description: Coastal-profile views by F. W. Beechey along the shores of Barrow's Strait and Bathurst Island, published by John Murray in 1821.

title: Survey of Winter Harbour, Melville Island, June 1820
description: Detailed manuscript-style survey chart of Winter Harbour with soundings, the shoal ground, the leading marks used to bring the ships in, and the shore observatory's fixed position (latitude 74 degrees 47 minutes 10 seconds N, longitude 110 degrees 26 minutes 13 seconds W); the tide table in the corner matches Appendix VII.

title: Situation of H.M. Ships Hecla and Griper, from the 17th to the 23rd of August 1820
description: Westall's engraving, after a sketch by Lieutenant Hoppner, of the two ships beset among ice floes during the difficult passage east after breaking free of Winter Harbour in August 1820.

title: Esquimaux of the Inlet called the River Clyde, West Coast of Baffin's Bay
description: Westall's engraving, after sketches by Lieutenants Beechey and Hoppner, of Inuit encountered at the inlet called the River Clyde on the west coast of Baffin's Bay during the 1819 outward passage.
